note: Hand-written expectations for src/lex/bindings.mjs. Each case names its input and what the analysis must say about it: `bindings` as name:kind in declaration order, `refs` as name->index where the index is into that binding list and `free` means the reference resolved to nothing, `deps` as specifier|form|bindings, and `unresolved` as the deduplicated global names. Fields left out are not checked, so a row can be about one thing. Like the token table next door this lives in JSON because many of its cases are import statements and tools/verify.mjs reads .mjs files looking for exactly that shape.

cases.why: the plain case: one name in, one use of it
a default import is a binding that carries its specifier
a renamed named import binds the local name and remembers the exported one
cases.in:
import { red as r, blue } from 'chalk';
r(blue);

cases.why: a namespace import, where `as` is grammar and not a reference
a bare import introduces no name and is still a dependency
an import attribute clause is data, so `with` and `type` read nothing
cases.in:
import data from './x.json' with { type: 'json' };
data.a;

cases.why: a dynamic import binds nothing, and the specifier is still a rewrite target
import.meta is not an import statement
a re-export names the other module's exports, which are nobody's references here
cases.in: export { a, b as c } from './b.mjs';

cases.why: an export clause with no `from` does mention local names
the loader call, whose binding carries the specifier the same way an import's does
a destructured loader call binds each name to the same specifier
a loader call nobody assigned is taken for its side effect and binds nothing
a parameter shadows an outer name, so the two mentions mean different things
a parameter and a body declaration share one scope, so the first wins the slot
cases.in: function f(a) { let b = a; return b; }

cases.why: a var reaches the whole function, not the block it was written in
cases.in: function f() { if (x) { var v = 1; } return v; }

cases.why: a let does not leave its block, so the mention after it resolves to nothing
an arrow's parameters are its own, and the walk saw them before the arrow said so
cases.in:
const f = (a, b) => a + b;
f(1);

cases.why: a single unparenthesised parameter
a concise body ends at the comma that belongs to the call around it
curried arrows nest their scopes
cases.in: const f = a => b => a + b;

cases.why: an async arrow: `async` is a modifier even though the tokens start like a call
a default value is an expression, so its names are references and not bindings
cases.in: function f(a = b, { c = d } = {}) { return a + c; }

cases.why: a renamed destructuring binds the value name, not the key
cases.in:
const { a: b, ...rest } = o;
b; rest;

cases.why: an array pattern with a hole and a default
a catch parameter binds in a scope of its own
a for head binds into the loop, including a body with no braces
a braced loop body sees the head's binding and nothing after the loop does
cases.in:
for (let n = 0; n < 3; n += 1) { f(n); }
n;

cases.why: object keys are not references and shorthand values are
cases.in:
const o = { a: 1, b() {}, c };
o.a;

cases.why: an accessor named after its own modifier word
cases.in: const o = { get get() { return 1; }, set set(v) {} };

cases.why: a computed key is an expression, so the name in it is read
class members, private fields and `this` are not references to anything
cases.in:
class A { #p = 1; m() { return this.#p; } static s = 2; }
new A();

cases.why: a heritage clause reads a name
a method's parameters belong to the method
a label is not a name in use, at either end
a property access is not a reference, through an optional chain either
a name inside a template substitution is read
a function expression's body is a scope even without a name
two uses of one dependency are two references to one binding
a local name shadows an imported one, which is why a rename needs the scope tree
several specifiers in one file, in source order

unanalysable.why: a loader call with a computed specifier
a loader call with a template
a dynamic import with a variable
a dynamic import with a joined string
